video_title: LONG VOL: THE EMPTIEST ROOM AROUND (Guest: Robert Mullin)
gist: Robert Mullin of Marathon Resource Advisors explains how his resource-focused long/short fund uses shorts and cheap long volatility (VIX calls, TLT calls, long yen) to preserve optionality, and argues a regime shift toward higher inflation and supply-constrained commodities favors energy (North Sea, tankers), selective copper and rare earths, and gold on a central-bank pivot.

themes.theme: Shorts and long vol as path-function tools

insights.claim: Marathon Resource Advisors argues the long/short book's main job is shaping the path of returns, not just the endpoint: shorts and long volatility let the fund stay uncorrelated or anti-correlated ('crisis alpha') in market disruptions.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: Judge a long/short manager on drawdown behaviour and crisis alpha rather than only the long-book picks.

insights.claim: A classic AW Jones structure (150% gross long, 75% gross short) still pays off even if the shorts lose: with a long book up 200%, losing 20% on a 75% gross short costs only about 15 points, and the short book mainly matters because it keeps the PM from degrossing in drawdowns.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: Evaluate shorts by their portfolio purpose and cost, not stand-alone P&L.

insights.claim: Being able to hold shorts and volatility lets a manager play offense when others are forced to degross: Marathon buys sustainable 7-10% dividend yield resource stocks as yields spike to 12-18% in a short volatile window, which can add thousands of basis points to annual returns.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: Dry powder plus hedges converts volatility spikes into entry points for high-yield resource names.

insights.claim: Dedicated short sellers and long-vol specialists have largely disappeared (Chanos-type shops closed, long-vol names like Chris Cole and Diego Pareja are only heard from briefly in 2000, 2020 and tariff episodes), and pods are shifting to shorting big index names or ETFs; the speaker treats silence about long-vol as a reason to start paying attention.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: A crowd-free long-vol and short space may mean cheap convexity and less competition on single-name shorts.

insights.claim: Non-fundamental flows (passive flows, tax-loss-harvesting long/short strategies) have made traditional shorting of large index constituents hard; example: Deere had about 15 straight quarters of guiding down while the stock re-rated higher.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: Large-cap index members can stay disconnected from fundamentals; narrative follows price.

insights.claim: Marathon has adapted its shorts by cutting positions by half or two-thirds when they move 10% against it, avoiding index-member names and shorting outside the index ($0.5-2 billion market cap style names), and using baskets of about ten names per subsector (7-10% of book) for liquidity and diversification.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: Short baskets outside the index reduce squeeze and index-flow risk.

insights.claim: Allocators have tried to eradicate volatility from every sleeve and want portfolios of low-vol components, making long volatility 'the emptiest room around'; Cliff Asness's AQR paper in praise of high-volatility alternatives argues truly uncorrelated or anti-correlated volatility should be embraced.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: A small anti-correlated high-vol sleeve can offset large damage elsewhere while being unloved by allocators.
insights.quote: I think Longvall may be the emptiest room around

insights.claim: Marathon runs a long-volatility book of about 1.5-2% of the portfolio, built from many instruments: VIX calls and call spreads, out-of-the-money options in currencies, commodities, ETFs and high yield, and utilities (bond-like vol early in a correction, stock-like later, giving a cheap step-function in vol).
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: The budget is fixed and diversified across instruments so the wrong instrument choice does not defeat the hedge.

insights.claim: The current hedge bucket includes TLT calls and long yen (against both euro and dollar); yen was chosen as the most overloaded funding-currency trade, and the euro leg reflects concern about French credit risk.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: Long yen and long-bond calls are being used as cheap risk-off hedges; host calls yen vs euro the year's home-run trade.

themes.theme: Regime change: inflation, geopolitics and portfolio design

insights.claim: The 25-year regime that rewarded long-duration assets, S&P 500 concentration, cheap leverage and 401k inflows is ending; the legacy allocation (private equity, private credit, multi-trillion-dollar sovereign and asset managers) is hard to rotate because there is little market cap in the assets they would need to buy.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: The potential 'earthquake' is forced reallocation out of long-duration, US-centric assets into scarce real assets.

insights.claim: The shift from a US-centric unipolar world to supply-chain resilience and national self-sufficiency (Ukraine, Russia/China/North Korea alignment) implies structurally higher inflation, making bonds less useful at 3-4% inflation than at 1.5-3%, and favoring a '60/20/20' mix with gold and energy over 60/40 (credited to Louis-Vincent Gave).
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: Position for a 3-4% inflation world: add gold and energy sleeves rather than relying on bonds as the hedge.

insights.claim: Simultaneous fiscal deficits across governments (no longer only the US since about 2010-2024, with Trump changing attitudes to deficits) are 'baked into the cake' for higher inflation.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Global fiscal expansion adds to the case for real assets over duration.

insights.claim: The current resource bull market is supply driven, unlike the demand-driven 2000-2012 boom: by Mullin's numbers resource-sector capex is down about 50% nominal and about 75% inflation adjusted since 2012-2014, and the projects needed for 2025-2035 production should have been started around 2020.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: Capital-starved supply makes price responses to demand sharper; supply-constrained commodities are favored.
insights.quote: Where we are currently is, you're absolutely correct, a supply driven bull market.

insights.claim: Three pillars underpin the resource bull: the capex gap, a tech/AI build-out that is much more materials-intensive than the 2000 tech boom, and a geopolitical imperative for countries to hold their own supply, which adds spending on top of catch-up.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: Resource exposure is a hedged way to own AI capex intensity.

insights.claim: China acts as a counter-cyclical buyer in resources: a decelerator at $105-110 Brent and an aggressive inventory rebuilder at $70-75, which Mullin finds spectacular for his energy equity case.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: Watch for Chinese restocking on oil dips as a floor and for a demand catalyst in commodities.

insights.claim: China deliberately popped its property bubble (Evergrande-era builders cut off, bankruptcies and jail accepted) to protect social stability; with growth at the low end of its 30-40 year range, the downside is digested and upside on pro-growth policy (infrastructure, domestic AI data centers) is nearly one-sided.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: Chinese stimulus is a free option for resource names already priced for weakness.
insights.quote: effectively, China is the world's largest commodity hedge fund

insights.claim: Energy was egregiously underowned in Q4 2025 (about 2.7% of the S&P 500, consensus of $50 or even $40s oil) before the geopolitical shock; the more lasting effect of the Strait of Hormuz disruption was depleting global oil buffers (US SPR, China) that had supported the $60 oil price.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: The thesis rests on inventory depletion, not on headlines about the strait opening or closing.

insights.claim: Mullin underestimated how flexible the global system was in absorbing a 10-15% cut in oil demand, but concludes energy is important again for data centers, AI, national security and political survival.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: Energy demand from AI infrastructure and security needs supports the sector.

insights.claim: Anti-fossil-fuel sentiment peaked around 2022-2024 and is giving way to 'energy pragmatism'; Marathon buys energy in jurisdictions with bad policy betting policy gets 'less stupid', e.g. UK North Sea producers burdened by about 80% windfall taxes at 2-3x cash flow and 15% dividend yields (a Darwinian, independent group with few names left).
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: Policy normalization in North Sea and Latin America is a catalyst-light value trade.

insights.claim: Canada under Carney is described as proving a pragmatic energy politician (carbon tax removed); Marathon likes Canadian energy names that grow, pay down debt and pay big dividends, with long-held positions though small current exposure.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: Canadian cash-return energy names fit the high-dividend resource framework.

insights.claim: Tanker markets are extreme: VLCC Middle East-Gulf Coast spot rates have done about four times as well as US Gulf Coast refining cracks, with daily rates of $800,000-1.2 million versus about $25,000 cost, one-year charters at $125-150k and two-year above $100k; a 10-year-old tanker can sell for about $160 million against about $125 million for a new build.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: Margin expansion is enormous but Mullin expects rates not to stay here; selecting the right tanker company matters.

insights.claim: Marathon favored tankers for almost two years as a hedge for its long energy book (OPEC supply increases hurt energy longs but help shipping), but did not own the spot-rate ETF; Mullin stresses tanker stocks vary wildly in VLCC exposure, Middle East operations and forward fixing, so single-name selection and following specialists matters.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: Don't buy the tanker that has lagged most; check VLCC exposure and freight sold forward.

themes.theme: Metals: copper, rare earths and gold

insights.claim: Marathon is short large-cap diversified miners and copper majors on the margin (economic headwinds, low-conviction 'AI bro' holders) while wanting a basket of the half-dozen high-quality next-generation copper development projects in good jurisdictions that could interest majors.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: Own the scarce projects, short the crowded majors.

insights.claim: Copper has held up while gold was hit partly because large US stockpiles built ahead of potential tariffs are viewed as strategic and cover up high US inventories; data-center demand helps only at the margin and China construction is the real swing factor.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: US stockpile effects may be distorting copper pricing signals.

insights.claim: In rare earths the bottleneck is processing rather than mining, deposits differ greatly in light versus heavy mix (making economics binary), and the space has become crowded as several countries offer guarantees and offtakes pulling hundreds of billions into an industry used to $5-10 billion capex, so oversupply 'winter is coming'; Mullin recalls uranium in the late 1990s going from six companies to 600 and back to about a dozen.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: Be discerning in strategic metals: favor scaled processors and expect a later shakeout.

insights.claim: Marathon cut gold weight after the 2025 run-up and 'silver eyes' on Twitter, tactically added into August 2026 when old-guard PMs were waiting for a $3,500 print, then trimmed as it spiked too fast; it needs central banks (especially the US) to 'blink' for the next leg.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: Next gold leg requires a policy pivot from hikes to cuts after the environment goes further than policymakers want.

insights.claim: Mullin frames Treasury Secretary Bessent as 'either you buy my bonds or I'll torch your equities, then you'll buy my bonds'; policymakers now have stronger bonds, a stable dollar and a stronger yen, so the next leg in gold comes when conditions overshoot what they want.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: Gold setup depends on policy overshoot; Marathon is 'sharpening pencils' on gold now.
insights.quote: I'll torch your equities and then you'll buy my bonds

insights.claim: Mullin's main investing weakness is being a dip buyer who wants to point to the exact low; after twenty years of reviewing entries he tries to wait until relative strength and absolute performance improve and the 'room' has one or two people in it.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: Waiting for confirmation costs some upside but improves entries in contrarian resource positions.

insights.claim: Portfolios should be built like architecture for the setting, as in Frank Lloyd Wright's floating Imperial Hotel in Tokyo surviving the 1923 earthquake; Mullin's goal is providing shelter in a storm via uncorrelated or anti-correlated returns, not the best raw returns.
insights.speaker: Robert Mullin
insights.so_what: Design for the coming regime, not the one that just worked.

insights.claim: Mullin and Muir suggest the biggest investor mistake is rigidity in framework and failing to recognize a changing backdrop.
insights.speaker: host and guest
insights.so_what: Re-test allocation assumptions as the macro regime shifts.
